chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Dollar's Rise to Dominance

lessons.title: The Dollar Today: SWIFT, Trade Invoicing, and Global Debt

body.text: The dollar has not been backed by gold since 1971, and it does not need to be. It is wired into the messaging system banks use to move money, the invoices exporters write, and the debt contracts borrowers sign, all over the world, including between countries that have nothing to do with the United States.

children.text: Lessons 1 and 2 covered how the dollar lost its gold anchor and found a new one in oil. This closing lesson of Chapter 3 brings the story up to the present. Today's dollar dominance no longer rests on any single mechanism, gold convertibility or an oil-pricing arrangement, it runs through the everyday infrastructure of global finance itself: the payment messaging network banks rely on, the currency most trade gets invoiced in, and the currency most international debt gets issued in.
SWIFT: The Plumbing Behind Global Payments

markDefs.definition: The Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, a Belgium-based messaging network that lets banks around the world securely instruct each other to move money. SWIFT does not move money itself; it carries the instructions that tell banks how to settle payments.

children.text: Most people picture SWIFT as a global payment system. It is more precise, and more useful for understanding its power, to think of it as the messaging layer banks use to instruct each other. When an Indian exporter gets paid by a European buyer, the actual movement of money happens through correspondent banking relationships, but the instruction that tells the buyer's bank to pay the exporter's bank typically travels over
. Founded in 1973, in the same turbulent stretch of monetary history as Lessons 1 and 2, SWIFT now connects more than 11,000 financial institutions across over 200 countries.

body.text: Chapter 1, Lesson 2 first raised the idea of the dollar payment system as sanctions leverage. SWIFT is precisely where that leverage gets applied in practice. Major Iranian banks were cut off from SWIFT in 2012 over nuclear-related sanctions, and major Russian banks were cut off in 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine. Neither action stopped Iran or Russia from transacting entirely, but both sharply raised the cost and friction of doing so, cutting them off from the fastest, most trusted rail in global finance. This is exactly why China, Russia, and others are actively building SWIFT alternatives like China's CIPS and Russia's SPFS, covered briefly later in this lesson and in depth in Chapter 4.

children.text: Trade Invoicing: The Dollar's Reach Beyond America

Chapter 1, Lesson 1 first flagged the gap between the US share of world trade, roughly a tenth of it, and the dollar's share of global trade invoicing, far higher. That gap has held remarkably steady for decades. A large share of trade between two countries that are neither the US, an Indian company importing electronics components from South Korea, for instance, still gets invoiced and settled in dollars, simply because both sides trust dollar pricing, dollar clearing, and dollar-denominated contracts more than any alternative.

children.text: Global Debt in Dollars: The Fed's Global Reach

The Bank for International Settlements tracks international debt securities, bonds and notes issued by borrowers outside their home country, and dollar-denominated debt consistently makes up the large majority, roughly 60 to 65% of the total. This includes plenty of borrowing that has nothing directly to do with the US: an Indonesian company issuing dollar bonds to European investors, for example. That is precisely why, as Chapter 1's lesson on the exorbitant privilege covered, a US Federal Reserve rate decision ripples through corporate and sovereign borrowing costs far outside America's own borders, including India's own corporate External Commercial Borrowings.

body.caption: Four pillars of dollar dominance today

body.text: Some economists describe this as a dollar smile: the dollar tends to strengthen both when the global economy is booming, because US assets attract growth-seeking capital, and when the global economy is in crisis, because investors flee to the dollar as the ultimate safe haven, exactly what happened during the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic. It is the middle ground, steady but unspectacular global growth, where the dollar tends to soften. Reserve currency status is not just about who wins in a crisis; it can mean winning in almost every scenario.

children.text: Cracks and Challengers: What's Being Built

None of this dominance is unchallenged. China launched its own Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, CIPS, in 2015 to support yuan-denominated trade settlement, still a fraction of SWIFT's volumes but growing steadily. Russia built its own System for Transfer of Financial Messages, SPFS, largely after being partially cut off from SWIFT. India has its own, more targeted response: an RBI circular from July 2022 permitted invoicing, payment, and settlement of exports and imports in rupees, aimed initially at facilitating trade with sanctions-hit Russia without routing payments through the dollar system at all. None of these alternatives come close to replacing the dollar's role yet, but each one is a direct, practical response to the sanctions leverage covered earlier in this lesson. Chapter 4 covers these challengers in full, including a dedicated look at what it would actually take for the rupee to go further down this road.

body.title: Explaining Sanctions Leverage to a Colleague
body.scenario: A colleague argues that cutting a country's banks off from SWIFT should not matter much, since SWIFT is just a messaging system and banks could presumably just call or email each other to arrange payments instead.
body.prompt: Using what this lesson covered about SWIFT's actual role and scale, how would you respond? What is genuinely lost when a country's major banks are removed from SWIFT, even though money can still theoretically move through other channels?
body.modelAnswer: Your colleague is right that SWIFT is a messaging network, not the money itself, so alternative channels do technically exist. What is actually lost is speed, standardisation, and above all trust at scale: SWIFT connects over 11,000 institutions using a common, secure, machine-readable format that lets banks automate and verify cross-border payments in seconds rather than negotiating bespoke, manual arrangements bank by bank. Losing SWIFT access forces a country's banks onto slower, more expensive, less trusted channels, and often makes foreign banks reluctant to deal with them at all for fear of running afoul of sanctions themselves, a chilling effect that goes well beyond the technical question of whether a message could theoretically be sent another way.

body.explanation: BIS data shows dollar-denominated debt consistently making up roughly 60 to 65% of international debt securities, far above the US share of the global economy, which is exactly why Federal Reserve policy decisions ripple through borrowing costs for companies and governments that have no direct link to the United States.

This lesson is educational content, not investment or policy advice.

points: SWIFT is a payment messaging network, not the money itself, connecting over 11,000 institutions across more than 200 countries, with the dollar carrying the largest single share of its messages

SWIFT's dominance is also its geopolitical leverage point, illustrated by Iran's 2012 and Russia's 2022 disconnections, which is a direct driver of alternatives like China's CIPS, Russia's SPFS, and India's own rupee trade settlement mechanism

The dollar's roughly 40-50% share of global trade invoicing and 60-65% share of international debt securities both far exceed the US share of world trade or GDP, reinforcing the pattern first raised in Chapter 1
The dollar smile idea captures how the dollar tends to strengthen in both boom and crisis conditions, arguably winning across most scenarios rather than just one

This closes Chapter 3's account of how the dollar built and reinforced its dominance since 1971; Chapter 4 turns to the euro, the Chinese yuan, and the rupee's own prospects as challengers to that dominance
